For each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] there is a corresponding point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)+2] with the same [MATH: x]-value and a [MATH: y]-value that is two units greater. So let's create a table of points.

Content:
Every point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)+2] is precisely two units above a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)]. The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)+2] is an upward vertical translation of the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by two units.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6e651a73afdcc2c9e4efd34e9e012678]

Content:
On the other hand, for each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] there is a corresponding point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)-2] with the same [MATH: x]-value and a [MATH: y]-value that is two units smaller. So let's create a table of points.

Content:
Every point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)-2] is two units below a point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)]. The graph of [MATH: y=f(x)-2] is a downward vertical translation of the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by two units.

items.title: Identifying Points that Must Lie on a Translated Curve

sections.normalized_html: The point [MATH: P] with coordinates [MATH: (3,4)] lies on the curve [MATH: y=f(x)]. Find a point that must lie on [MATH: y=f(x)+3]?
sections.readable_text: The point [MATH: P] with coordinates [MATH: (3,4)] lies on the curve [MATH: y=f(x)]. Find a point that must lie on [MATH: y=f(x)+3]?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Method 1

The graph of [MATH: y = f(x)+3] is obtained by translating the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: 3] units up.

Hence, if the point [MATH: (3,4)] lies on [MATH: y=f(x)], then the point [MATH: (3,4+3) = (3,7)] lies on [MATH: y=f(x) + 3.]

Method 2

As [MATH: (3,4)] lies on [MATH: y = f(x)], we have that [MATH: f(3) = 4.]

Now, if [MATH: x = 3] then

[MATH: y|= f(3) + 3; = 4 + 3; = 7.]

So, the point [MATH: (3,7)] must lie on [MATH: y = f(x) + 3.]
